## Become a Translator Contributor in WordPress and Translate User Registration Plugin

<https://docs.wpuserregistration.com/translation-and-localization/become-a-translator-contributor-in-wordpress-and-translate-user-registration-plugin>

Translate WordPress Plugins: User Registration Guide

# Become a Translator Contributor in WordPress and Translate User Registration Plugin
Learn how to become a WordPress translator and contribute to the User Registration plugin by joining translation teams and following the WordPress localization workflow.
Last updated on Jul 15, 2026

Would you like to contribute to the WordPress community by translating plugins into your native language?

User Registration & Membership is translation-ready and welcomes translator contributions from around the world. This tutorial will show you how to register as a WordPress translator, join translation teams, and translate the User Registration plugin using the WordPress translation ecosystem.

## Before Getting Started

Before getting started, make sure you have the following:

A WordPress.org account

Understanding of your target language and locale

Familiarity with translation guidelines and best practices

Access to the Translator's Handbook on WordPress.org

## Understanding WordPress Translation Roles

WordPress uses a structured translation system with specific roles:

General Translation Editor (GTE) — Manages translations for an entire locale across all projects

Project Translation Editor (PTE) — Approves translations for specific plugins or themes

Translator — Submits translation suggestions that require approval before going live

All translation suggestions must be reviewed and approved by Translation Editors before they appear on the live site. This ensures quality and consistency across the WordPress ecosystem.

So, lets begin.

## Step 1: Create a WordPress.org Account

Visit WordPress.org.

Click on the Register link in the top-right corner.

Complete the registration form with your username, email address, and a secure password.

Confirm your email to activate your account.

## Step 2: Familiarize Yourself with WordPress Translation

Visit the Translate WordPress site.

Read the Translator's Handbook to understand translation guidelines, tools, and best practices.

## Step 3: Find the Plugin to Translate

Go to the plugin's page on the WordPress.org Plugin Directory .

Scroll to the Languages section to check if the plugin has existing translations.

Click the Contribute Translation link to navigate to the plugin translation page.

## Step 4: Join a Translation Team (Optional but Recommended)

Identify the locale (language and region) you want to translate for.

Visit the Translation Teams page .

Contact the General Translation Editor (GTE) for your locale to express your contribution interest.

## Step 5: Start Translating

On the plugin's translation page:

Select your locale from the list of available languages.

You'll see a list of translation strings (text elements that require translation).

Click on a string to translate it.

Enter your translation in the provided field.

Save your suggestion.

## Step 6: Get Approval for Your Translations

Translation suggestions are reviewed by Translation Editors (PTEs or GTEs).

If you'd like to become a PTE for a specific plugin, contact the author or an existing editor for your locale and request access.

## Step 7: Translate the User Registration Plugin

Navigate to the User Registration Plugin page on WordPress.org.

Scroll to the Languages section and click the Contribute Translation link.

Follow the steps in Step 5 to translate the strings specific to the plugin.

## Step 8: Use Translation Tools

GlotPress: The WordPress translation platform is available at translate.wordpress.org.

Translation Editors: Tools like Poedit or Loco Translate can help you generate .po and .mo files, but suggestions must be submitted via GlotPress.

Glossaries and Style Guides: Use tools your locale team provides to ensure consistent translations.

## Step 9: Stay Active and Engaged

Regularly check for updates to the plugin that may require new translations.

Participate in discussions and forums within the Polyglots team .

Contribute to translating other parts of WordPress, such as themes, core, or documentation.

By following these steps, you can become an active translator contributor in the WordPress community and help make plugins like the User Registration Plugin accessible to a global audience.

## Loco Translation

<https://docs.wpuserregistration.com/translation-and-localization/translate-user-registration-to-another-language>

Translate User Registration Plugin with Loco Translate

# Loco Translation
Learn how to translate the User Registration & Membership plugin into any language using Loco Translate or WordPress.org contributions.
Last updated on Jul 15, 2026

Would you like to make your registration forms and membership pages available in multiple languages? User Registration & Membership is translation-ready, allowing you to translate the plugin into any language without modifying code. This tutorial will show you how to translate the plugin using Loco Translate or contribute translations through WordPress.org.

Before getting started, make sure you've installed and activated the User Registration & Membership plugin on your WordPress site.

## Translating with Loco Translate (Recommended)

Loco Translate is a WordPress plugin that provides a visual interface for translating plugins directly from your dashboard. This is the fastest way to translate User Registration & Membership for your site.

### Installing Loco Translate

To install Loco Translate, go to **Plugins > Add New** from your WordPress dashboard. Type 'Loco Translate' in the search bar. Once the plugin appears in the results, click **Install Now**, then click **Activate** after installation completes.

### Setting Up Your Translation

Once Loco Translate is active, navigate to **Loco Translate > Plugins** from your dashboard. Click on **User Registration and Membership** from the plugin list.

Click on **New Language.** Here, you'll see all available languages under 'WordPress language.' Choose your target language from the list.

Next, select the location for your translation file. We recommend choosing **languages/plugins/user-registration-.po** to preserve your translations during plugin updates. Click **Start translating** to set up the new language.

### Translating Plugin Text

In the translation interface, you'll see all translatable text from the plugin in the Source text window. Click any text in the Source text window to select it. Then, enter your translation in the translate window below the Source text. Click **Save** to store your translations.

Loco Translate automatically pulls all hardcoded texts from the plugin, so you don't need to search for strings manually. Simply, in the source text window, click on any of the text you want to translate. Then, move to the translate window below under the Source text window and insert the translation you want to provide.

Click on **save **after you are done translating the text to save the plugin settings and the translations for the required settings should be set.

### Verifying Your Translation

To verify your translations are working, go to **Settings > General** in your WordPress dashboard. Change the 'Site language' dropdown to the language you just translated.

Click **Save Changes**, then refresh any admin page to see your translations applied.

## Translating Email Notifications

<https://docs.wpuserregistration.com/translation-and-localization/translating-email-notifications>

Translate User Registration Email Notifications with WPML

# Translating Email Notifications
This guide explains how to configure WPML to automatically send User Registration & Membership email notifications in each visitor's preferred language.
Last updated on Aug 18, 2026

## Overview

This guide explains how to translate the emails sent by User Registration & Membership into other languages using WPML, one of the most widely used multilingual plugins for WordPress. The plugin already supports translated email content, but a multilingual plugin needs to be properly configured before those translations will actually appear to your visitors.

## How Email Translation Works

User Registration & Membership sends emails using the content you've configured under the plugin's Emails settings. On its own, the plugin only stores one version of that content. To show a different version to visitors browsing your site in another language, you need a plugin like WPML — it detects each visitor's selected language and swaps in the matching translated text whenever an email is generated.

## Prerequisites

User Registration & Membership plugin, installed and activated

WPML plugin, on the Multilingual CMS plan or higher (required for String Translation)

## Access Path

Text JavaScript TypeScript JSX TSX JSON PHP Python Bash HTML CSS SCSS SQL YAML Markdown Go Java Ruby Rust
`WPML → Languages
WPML → String Translation
WPML → Theme and Plugins Localization
User Registration & Membership → Settings → Emails`

## Step-by-Step Instructions

### Step 1: Install and Configure WPML

Install the following WPML plugins:

WPML Multilingual CMS

WPML String Translation

WPML Translation Management (optional)

Go to **WPML → Languages** and run the setup wizard.

Select your default language and the additional languages you want to support.

Choose a URL format (subdirectories are recommended), then save your changes.

### Step 2: Turn On String Detection

Go to **WPML → String Translation**.

Enable **Look for strings while pages are rendered**.

### Step 3: Register URM's Email Strings

You can register the plugin's translatable strings automatically or manually.

**Method A: Automatic Registration**

Go to **WPML → Theme and Plugins Localization**.

Click **Scan Selected Plugins for Strings**.

Select **User Registration & Membership** from the plugin list.

Click **Scan** to register all translatable strings.

**Method B: Manual Registration**

Create or open a page containing a form that triggers an email, such as your registration form.

Go to **Pages → All Pages**, then click the **+** icon next to that page to create a translated version. Complete and save the translation.

Register a test user account on that page. Then switch to each target language using the WPML language switcher and repeat the action that triggers the email (for example, registering again). This registers the email strings with WPML so they become available to translate.

### Step 4: Translate the Email Content

Go to **WPML → String Translation**.

Filter by domain, or search for strings containing "email," "mail," "message," or "notification." Email string names typically follow a pattern such as `user_registration_successfully_registered_email`.

Click the translation icon next to a string to open the translation field.

Enter your translation for each target language and save.

Keep all dynamic placeholders exactly as they appear in the original text — for example `{{username}}`, `{{site_name}}`, `{{activation_link}}`, `{{membership_plan}}`, and `{{expiry_date}}`. These are automatically replaced with real data when the email is sent, so changing or removing them will break the email.

### Step 5: Test Your Translations

Switch your site to each target language using the WPML language switcher.

Register a new test account and confirm the email arrives in the correct language.

Repeat this check for translated form fields and email subject lines using the same method.

## Additional Resources

How to resend a verification email

Fixing the WordPress "emails not sending" issue

## Closing

Once your email strings are registered and translated, User Registration & Membership will automatically send each visitor the correct language version based on their selected site language. If you add new email templates or form fields later, repeat Steps 3–5 to register and translate the new strings.

## WPML Translation

Translate Registration Forms with WPML Tutorial

# WPML Translation
Learn how to create multilingual registration forms and translate email notifications using WPML with User Registration & Membership plugin.
Last updated on Jul 15, 2026

Would you like to offer your registration forms in multiple languages to reach a global audience? User Registration & Membership is translation-ready and works seamlessly with WPML to create multilingual registration experiences.

This tutorial will show you how to translate your registration forms, email notifications, and form content into any language using WPML.

Before getting started, make sure you've installed and activated the User Registration & Membership plugin on your WordPress site. Then, make sure you've purchased and installed WPML Multilingual CMS (or higher plan) along with the WPML String Translation plugin.

## Installing and Configuring WPML

To begin translating your registration forms, you'll need to set up WPML on your WordPress site.

You can easily translate User Registration and your registration forms to multiple languages. For this, you can use any multilingual plugins such as WPML or Polylang. Here, we are using the WPML plugin which is the most popular Multilingual plugin for WordPress. So, go ahead and install the WPML plugin on your website.

After you install and activate the plugin on your site, you can see the **WPML **tab on your admin dashboard. Now, you need to set up the plugin here. First, you need to select the current language of your website.

Once activated, navigate to **WPML → Languages** in your WordPress dashboard. WPML will launch a setup wizard to help you configure your multilingual site.

## Setting Up Your Languages

The setup wizard will guide you through selecting your site's languages and URL structure.

First, select your site's default language - this is the language your content is currently written in. Then, click **Next** to add additional languages you want to translate your forms into. You can add as many languages as needed.

On the next screen, you can the change Language Switcher Options in the third step of the setup.

Click **Save** to complete the language setup.

## Enabling String Detection

WPML needs to detect translatable strings from the User Registration plugin before you can translate them.

Go to **WPML → String Translation** and locate the option **Select strings within domain**. Enable this setting—it allows WPML to automatically find translatable text as you use your site.

You can use two methods to register strings for translation: automatic scanning or manual triggering. We'll cover both approaches.

To add translations for these texts you can click on the translations and edit the translations.

You can easily edit the translations and **Save** them right here.

Now, go to the page where you have added your user registration form. You can see the **WPML’s Translation Editor.** Here, you can include the Translation languages for this document.

## Testing Your Translations

After you’re done with the translation Settings, you can update the page. The frontend view of the registration will look something like this.

Use the WPML language switcher on your site's frontend to change languages. Register a new test account in each language to confirm:

Form fields display in the correct language

Validation messages appear translated

Email notifications arrive in the user's selected language

Success messages and redirects work properly

If any strings appear untranslated, return to **WPML → String Translation** and verify the translation was saved correctly.
